title: Secondary Amenorrhoea - Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhoea
patient_instructions: You are Chloe Roberts, a 24-year-old competitive long-distance runner and part-time personal trainer. Your periods have stopped - your last period was about 7 months ago. Before that they were regular. You are NOT pregnant (you are not sexually active at present and a home test was negative). Over the last year you increased your training substantially (running 80-100 km per week plus gym) and have been eating a strict low-fat, calorie-restricted diet to 'stay lean' for competition; you have lost about 6 kg and people say you look very thin. If asked: you feel cold a lot, tired, and your mood is a bit flat, but you deny bingeing/purging. You have NO headaches, no visual problems, no milky nipple discharge, no excess hair growth or acne. No hot flushes. No thyroid symptoms. No new medications, no contraception. Your ideas: you think stopping periods is 'normal for athletes' and maybe even convenient. Your concerns: only mild - a friend said missing periods could affect your bones or your ability to have children one day. Your expectation: reassurance so you can keep training. You are pleasant and a little dismissive of the problem. If the candidate asks about eating patterns, admit you restrict food quite tightly and fear gaining weight.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Chloe Roberts, a 24-year-old elite-level runner, presents with 7 months of absent periods (previously regular). Her urine pregnancy test today is negative. In 8 minutes: take a focused history to determine the cause of her secondary amenorrhoea, form a working diagnosis, and briefly explain to her what you think is going on and what you would do next. You do not need to examine the patient.
examiner_instructions: This tests a structured secondary amenorrhoea history that, after excluding pregnancy, identifies functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea (low FSH/LH/oestrogen pattern) driven by the female athlete triad / relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S). Reward exclusion of pregnancy first, then a systematic differential screen: PCOS (hirsutism/acne), thyroid, hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea, headache, visual field defect), premature ovarian insufficiency (hot flushes), and drugs/Depo-Provera. Reward an eating/exercise and energy-availability assessment (a validated screen such as SCOFF) and recognition of bone-health risk. The candidate should describe this as reversible subfertility (fertility usually returns with restored energy balance) - NOT permanent infertility. Reward mention of first-line management: multidisciplinary energy restoration and DEXA for prolonged hypo-oestrogenaemia, and MRI if red-flag pituitary symptoms. Prompt: 'What is the biochemical pattern you expect and why?'

criteria: Excludes pregnancy first, then takes a full menstrual/contraceptive history (including Depo-Provera)
Assesses exercise load, dietary restriction, weight loss and energy availability (female athlete triad/RED-S) with an eating-disorder screen (e.g. SCOFF)
Screens differentials: PCOS, thyroid, hyperprolactinaemia and premature ovarian insufficiency
Names functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea as the working diagnosis
Explains the expected hypogonadotropic pattern (low FSH/LH/oestrogen, normal TSH/prolactin)
Frames the fertility impact as reversible subfertility, not permanent infertility
First-line management: multidisciplinary energy restoration (dietitian +/- psychologist), reduce exercise, restore weight
Requests DEXA for bone density given >6 months hypo-oestrogenaemia; considers transdermal oestradiol with cyclical progestogen if prolonged
Red-flag safety-net: image the pituitary (MRI) if headache, visual field defect or galactorrhoea
Explains diagnosis in lay terms and engages a potentially dismissive patient
Checks understanding and negotiates a realistic plan

red_flags: Headache, visual field defect or galactorrhoea suggesting a prolactinoma/sellar lesion - image the pituitary (MRI) despite normal prolactin
Features of an eating disorder / severe energy deficiency (rapid weight loss, cold intolerance, low mood, purging) requiring urgent multidisciplinary care
Prolonged (>6 months) hypo-oestrogenaemia risking osteoporosis and stress fractures
Hot flushes/vasomotor symptoms raising premature ovarian insufficiency as an alternative diagnosis
australian_guidelines: eTG / RANZCOG functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea: first-line management is a multidisciplinary approach (dietitian +/- psychologist) with reduced exercise load and restored energy balance rather than starting the COCP
For prolonged amenorrhoea, transdermal oestradiol with cyclical progestogen is preferred over the COCP for bone protection; arrange a DEXA scan given osteoporosis risk
Screen for the female athlete triad / relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) and use a validated eating-disorder screen (e.g. SCOFF)
Exclude pregnancy first in any woman with secondary amenorrhoea (RACGP), then investigate FSH/LH/oestradiol, TSH and prolactin
learning_objectives: Take a structured secondary amenorrhoea history that excludes pregnancy and screens the key differentials
Recognise functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea and its hypogonadotropic biochemical pattern
Counsel that fertility is usually reversible with restored energy balance and address bone-health risk
Identify pituitary red flags mandating MRI despite normal prolactin
key_points: Always exclude pregnancy first in secondary amenorrhoea
Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea shows low FSH/LH/oestrogen with normal TSH/prolactin and is driven by energy deficit
It causes reversible subfertility, not permanent infertility - fertility usually returns with restored energy balance
First-line management is energy restoration (dietitian +/- psychologist) and reduced exercise, not the COCP; arrange DEXA for bone health
MRI pituitary if headache, visual field defect or galactorrhoea

citations.claim: Prolonged hypo-oestrogenaemia from amenorrhoea reduces bone mineral density (osteoporosis), supporting bone-health assessment in this presentation.
citations.source: Talley and O'Connor's Clinical Examination, 8th edition (Elsevier Australia 2017), p.511

citations.claim: A gynaecological history for amenorrhoea should cover menstrual history, previous contraception (especially Depo-Provera), intra-abdominal/genitourinary surgery and exercise/eating patterns.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2782

citations.claim: Core menstrual history documentation includes age of onset, regularity, date of last period and associated dysmenorrhoea/menorrhagia.
